newsitem.title: FRANCE: Kouchner to quit French politics for Sudan aid.
newsitem.headline: Kouchner to quit French politics for Sudan aid.

text.p: Former minister Bernard Kouchner, founder of the medical aid charity Medecins sans Frontieres and a champion of humanitarian intervention, said on Tuesday he was quitting French politics and going to Sudan to care for the ill and destitute.
Embittered after failing to find a constituency for next year's general election, Kouchner, 57, said he would return to his first career of humanitarian medicine.

He told France Inter radio he would make his last political appearance at a congress of his small Radical Socialist Party on March 8, then, "In the evening I will leave for southern Sudan where I have an hospital, to care for people in misery".
"I have been very unhappy. My friends have stabbed me in the back," he said.

A former health and humanitarian affairs minister under the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand, Kouchner suffered a severe defeat in a parliamentary by-election in the Marseille suburb of Gardanne last October.

Faced with opposition from the dominant Socialist party, the Radical Socialists failed to find him a constituency for the 1998 election. Several provincial selection boards turned down the Parisian intellectual as an electoral liability.
"Let's drop this. They used to come look for me when I was popular. Now that I am less popular and I'm asking something for myself, they keep me away," Kouchner said.
France's most popular cabinet minister in the early 1990s, Kouchner was once seen as a possible presidential candidate. His fortunes slipped after the Socialists lost power in 1993.
But he remains a member of the European parliament, to which he was elected as an independent on the Socialist list in 1994.

A gastro-enterologist, Kouchner founded Medecins sans Frontieres in 1971 and, a decade later, its sister organisation Medecins du Monde. The groups' aid workers became known all over the Third World as "the French Doctors".
He joined the cabinet in 1988, campaigning in international bodies to establish the right to humanitarian intervention.
When famine and civil war in Somalia reached its height in December 1992, he personally carried a bag of rice ashore into the capital Mogadishu.
The gesture, performed before a clutch of television crews, caused a furore back home, where a critical press and some Socialist allies denounced it as self-promotion.
Critics said the problem in Somalia was not a lack of food aid, but an inability to prevent armed gangs from stealing it.
Kouchner was pugnaciously unrepentant. But in his interview on Tuesday, he said the episode had left him deeply wounded.
"Coming from the Socialists, it hurt me. I found them vile," he said.
